Job roles

Quizlet Match

3. Registered nurses (RN) Connect

Deliver top-quality clinical care in the residential facility, which includes:

  • Checking the health and well-being of older individuals to catch any changes early for better health results.
  • Leading in the delivery of care.
  • Managing and overseeing enrolled nurses and care workers by coordinating, delegating, and supervising their tasks.
  • Administering and managing medications following medical guidelines.
  • Taking care of wounds.
  • Infection prevention and control

The RN is responsible for reporting to the clinical nurse (CN) or the clinical manager (CM).

As an RN, more advanced roles can be undertaken such as the care coordinator, who organises the care for the older people, or the role of director of nursing, whose responsibility is to oversee all service and care delivery of the staff.

*CHCAGE013*

4. Enrolled nurse (EN)

  • Enrolled Nurses (ENs) work under the guidance of Registered Nurses (RNs) and have more complex roles than Assistant in Nursing (AINs).
  • Their responsibilities involve providing a higher level of clinical care than AINs, which includes monitoring and reporting vital signs to RNs or doctors.
  • They are responsible for wound care.
  • They assist with pre and post-operative care in a hospital setting.
  • ENs write detailed records, follow care plans, and attend to the personal hygiene of older individuals.
  • They also administer medications.
  • ENs are responsible for their practice and must comply with the Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia's requirements.
  • To become an Enrolled Nurse, individuals must complete a Diploma of Nursing.

*CHCAGE013*

5. Assistant in Nursing (AIN)

  • AIN’s provide support to other nurses such as setting up for procedures and cleaning up afterwards
  • Assisting with rehab exercises and basic treatment,
  • Applying simple wound dressings,
  • Assisting with the activities of daily living for the older person
  • Maintaining accurate patient records.
  • The qualification for this position is a Certificate III in Health Services Assistance

6. Health service assistant (HSA)

  • Provides support to other nurses and allied health professionals
  • Assists in the planning of daily routines.
  • The care provided by the HSA includes assisting with rehabilitation exercises as directed by the RN,
  • Setting up for any procedures as required by an RN,
  • Cleaning equipment,
  • Applying simple wound dressings,
  • Maintaining accurate records as well as assisting with the activities of daily living of the older person.
  • They sit under the supervision and delegation of the RN and report to them. The qualification for an HSA is the Certificate III in Health Services Assistance.

7. Lifestyle and leisure worker

These workers organise activities including craft, bingo, music, or other activities, which assist the older people both mentally and physically and provide opportunities for social interaction.

Work with volunteers and therapists to design and deliver a variety of programs which individuals can choose to attend including gentle exercise, craft, music and other activities

*CHCAGE013*

A Lifestyle Worker also does personal care, helps with community activities, follows individual plans, collaborates with visiting therapists, and carries out therapy programs.

Reports to Team Leader

*CHCDIS020*

8. Support worker Job Description of Support Worker

Within the residential aged care setting the responsibilities of the support worker include:

  • personal care needs of the resident such as toileting, showering and dressing
  • assisting the resident with mobility needs
  • supporting the older person with skills to maintain independence
  • food and fluid support for the resident
  • providing conversation and companionship
  • care that is culturally appropriate
  • support that complies with WHS requirements
  • using computers for documentation and reporting of resident's needs..

*CHCAGE013*

9. Support worker

For a support worker providing homecare services in the person's home, the role is similar but there are some additional supports that may be provided.

Assistance to the elderly person may include cleaning, cooking and transport for shopping or appointments.

The scope of practice of the support worker includes the full range of functions, responsibilities and activities that the person has been educated in and is competent to perform. The scope is set by the professional standards which falls under the appropriate legislation.

A job description is one way of identifying what is involved in the support worker's role in the workplace, but it is always reasonable to speak to the supervisor to clarify any questions about this role.

10. Support worker

Examples of a request from a person that the Support Worker wouldn't be able to handle because it falls outside their usual duties includes:

  • an older person asking for help with managing their finances,
  • seeking advice on medications,
  • needing assistance with wound care or dressing changes,
  • or requesting toenail cutting, or similar tasks.

*CHCAGE013*

11. Physiotherapist

  • Assess and assist the older person with exercise regimes and manual therapy in musculoskeletal, neurological and respiratory conditions

*CHCAGE013* / *CHCDIS020*

12. Podiatrist

  • Assess and care for feet such as trimming toenails, prescribing footwear and also managing any foot conditions particularly in diabetes and arthritis

*CHCAGE013*

13. Occupational Therapist

  • Assist with the development of new skills for personal care and activities of daily living following injury or illness, accessing equipment as needed for the older person and recommending home modifications as required.

*CHCAGE013* / *CHCDIS020*

14. Speech Pathologist

  • Work with individuals who may have difficulties with swallowing, communication, speech or language. This may be because of the ageing process or result from injury or accident

*CHCAGE013* / *CHCDIS020*

15. Social Worker

  • Offer counselling services or may refer to other specialists to assist the individual to manage social or personal issues

*CHCAGE013* / *CHCDIS020*

16. Dietician

  • Assist with information on diet, nutrition, supplementation and menu planning to improve health outcomes. They also help the individual to manage health conditions including diabetes, obesity and food intolerances or allergies.

*CHCAGE013*

17. Psychiatrist

  • A trained medical doctor who is able to 'diagnose, treat and prevent mental, emotional and behavioural disorders' and can prescribe medications to support the person. *CHCDIS020*

18. Psychologist

  • Human behaviour specialists who help with a range of mental health problems and help people facing a range of life challenges. *CHCDIS020*

20. Certain conditions must be satisfied by the Registered Nurse before delegation is allowed

20. Certain conditions must be satisfied by the Registered Nurse before delegation is allowed.

  • Talking with all the people involved,
  • Getting permission from the older person or their decision maker,
  • Do a risk assessment,
  • Teaching the worker about the task, and
  • Making sure the worker is skilled for that task.

The Registered Nurse also needs to watch over the worker when they're doing the task.

*CHCAGE013*

21. Code of conduct

21. Code of conduct Connect

The purpose of the code is to improve the health, safety and quality of life of the ageing individual by encouraging honest and respectful behaviour towards them and protecting them against workers who may pose an unacceptable risk of harm. In this way the individual's trust in the service can be enhanced (ACQSC, 2022, Code of Conduct for Aged Care).

23 Scope of Practice

23. Discussion

If a Registered Nurse asked you to do something that you didn't feel skilled enough to do or that seemed out of your scope of practice, what action would you take as a Personal Care Worker?

Tell the nurse you don't feel confident doing the task and ask for more training before you try it and when it is out of your scope of practice - inform the RN it is out of you scope of practice

*CHCAGE013*

24. culturally competency

24. What does culturally competency look like? Connect CHCAGE013 And Connect CHCDIS020

  • Being good at getting along with people from different cultures at work and in your personal life.
  • Knowing and caring about your own cultural beliefs and also respecting what other people believe.
  • Enjoying how diverse cultures make life interesting and exciting.

*CHCAGE013*

25. Individualised support plans

25. Individualised support plans Connect CHCAGE013 And Connect CHCDIS020

The Individualised plan tells us what help an older person needs. It guides the services and support they get.

This plan helps all the caregivers give the same kind of help to the older person.

The plan is made together with the older person, their family, doctor, nurses, and other health experts if needed. But it should mainly show what the older person wants and thinks.

The person needs to agree to the plan before it's put into action.

*CHCAGE013* / *CHCDIS020*

26. Individualised support plan contains *CHCDIS020*

  • Client goals, (NB)
  • special interests,
  • interventions,
  • evaluation,
  • mobility needs,
  • communication needs,
  • activities of daily living,
  • social needs,
  • religious preferences
  • key strengths and abilities

there must always be review and evaluation of the care plan and it will need to change to reflect changing situations. (NB)

*CHCAGE013*

  • Personal information
  • medical history including allergies
  • personalised needs and goals that the client wishes to pursue
  • functional impairment
  • mobility requirement
  • activities of daily living
  • nutrition or any required assistance with meals
  • religious, cultural, social or spiritual considerations
  • special interests

27. Reporting and documentation

27. Reporting and documentation Connect

  • clear
  • concise
  • legible
  • accurate
  • meet legal requirements
  • include any information about changes of the client and any assessment made of them.
  • Keep record what the client needs for their care.
  • Good records can protect us in case of legal problems.
  • We follow rules for writing down care information in Aged Care Quality Standards.
  • Share what we know so all staff understand how to help.
  • Prove we provided the services the client needed.
  • Quickly report any changes in the client's condition for fast help.
  • Make sure everyone gives the same care because we all know what's happening.

WHS

29. Hazards vs Risk Connect

Hazard

A hazard is something that has the potential cause harm or danger

Example – Slippery floor

Risk

Risk is the likelihood that harm may result from a hazard

Example - the likelihood of someone slipping and falling on the slippery floor.

The difference is that a hazard is the potential for harm, while a risk is the actual likelihood of that harm happening.

*CHCAGE013*

30. Support work role with regards to risks

30.

The support worker has the responsibility to

  • alert the supervisor about any hazards or risks they spot,
  • adhere to workplace health and safety Policies and procedures,
  • participate in safety training,
  • ensure they are well-rested before starting their shift.

*CHCAGE013*

31. Risks in the homecare setting

31. Risks in the homecare setting

  • The carer may be exposed to - Hazardous manual tasks – awkward postures such as making a low bed, spending a long period of time without a break doing a repetitious task (e.g. mopping a large area), or working in a limited space to provide personal support. *CHCDIS020*
  • Risks involved in food handling or food preparation.
  • Chemical injuries – these can result from the use of chemical substances for cleaning especially in areas with poor ventilation.
  • Injury from motor vehicle accidents – risks occur in this area due to poor road conditions, distraction from the person's behaviour, poorly maintained vehicle or rushing due to a changed work schedule.
  • Work-related violence – risks may come from the elderly person's actions, their carers or anyone else in the home at the time of service provision.
  • Risk of infection from contact with animal excreta.
  • Slips and trips that result from uneven flooring, loose mats, or obstacles.

*CHCAGE013*

2. Risks outside of the Home when assisting a person with shopping

32.2 Risks outside of the Home, when assisting a person with shopping

  • assisting clients in and out of cars and managing bags of food or parcels
  • Being cautious in places with loud noises and busy crowds
  • accessing buildings where mobility is an issue for the client
  • access to toilet facilities and possible infection risks
  • slippery or uneven surfaces in the footpath or building *CHCDIS020*
  • exposure to wild animals in a park or rural setting
  • isolation if some issue occurred with the client either physical or behavioural.

Consider environmental factors like sun exposure, staying hydrated, temperature regulation, and accessible pathways. *CHCDIS020*

3. Risks outside of the Home, in community centre activities

32.3 Risks outside of the Home, in community centre activites

  • Check the activity area for any safety risks
  • Make sure tools and equipment are safe to use.
  • Confirm the person is physically able to take part in the activity.
  • Consider who else will be involved in the activity.
  • Be aware of any relationship or social issues that may affect participation.
  • Being cautious in places with loud noises and busy crowds
  • accessing buildings where mobility is an issue for the client
  • access to toilet facilities and possible infection risks

*CHCAGE013*

When Planning an Activity, Collecting info about an activity to assess risks *CHCDIS020* - Connect CHCDIS020

35. Key organisations within the sector

35. Key organisations within the sector Connect

  • Queensland Community Care Network (QCCN):
    Connects volunteers with older people to build meaningful friendships and alleviate loneliness in aged care homes.
  • Older Persons Advocacy Network (OPAN):
    Advocacy organization helping older people understand and exercise their rights, resolving issues with aged care providers.
  • Dementia Australia:
    Provides information and support for people with dementia, families, and carers through a helpline and counseling. Offers education for health professionals on understanding and supporting those with dementia.
  • Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW):
    Develops and maintains statistical data on health and welfare issues, supporting service delivery decisions and better policies.
  • Diabetes Australia:
    Offers information and support for those with diabetes, emphasizing prevention. Provides updates on research and best practices for health professionals.
  • Continence Foundation of Australia:
    Provides information on continence issues for individuals and guidance for carers, families, and health professionals.
  • Palliative Care Australia:
    National peak body for palliative care, collaborating with consumers and supporting aged care and other sectors providing relief for people with life-limiting illnesses.
  • Carers Gateway:
    Australian Government program offering free services and support for carers, including peer support groups, counseling, and emergency respite.
  • My Aged Care:
    Provides information on the Commonwealth Home Support Program and Home Care Packages for aging individuals.

*CHCAGE013*

36. Self-care

36. Self-care Connect CHCAGE013 And Connect CHCDIS020

What can you do to decrease the impact of stress in your life?

Connect

Strategies to Monitor Stress: *CHCDIS020*

  • Recognize your own stress responses, like changes in sleep patterns and mood.
  • Be aware of causes of workplace stress, such as workload or dealing with people with complex behaviors.
  • Consider your health; are you frequently unwell or tired?
  • Reflect on how you react to people around you, noting impatience or anger.
  • Evaluate if you've experienced critical incidents and if debriefing was offered.

Self-Care Strategies for Workplace Stress:

  • Practice meditation, yoga, exercise, self-talk, and relaxation techniques.
  • Engage in professional development related to workplace stress or specific challenges.
  • Seek guidance from a workplace mentor to cope with stress.
  • Utilize the organization's Employee Assistance Scheme.
  • Maintain a balanced diet, enjoy activities you like, and ensure you get enough rest.

If self-care strategies don't reduce workplace stress: *CHCDIS020*

  • Follow organization policies: Seek support from your workplace by discussing it with your supervisor.
  • Access professional support: Use the Employee Assistance Program or consult with a psychologist, following organization guidelines.

37. Psychosocial disability

Connect

37. Nature of Psychosocial disability

Psychosocial disability can come and go, like episodes. Sometimes, when it happens, a person might need extra help. It usually happens because someone with a mental health issue faces problems in their social environment that make things difficult for them, and they feel stuck because of these problems.

Psychosocial disability can interact with other disabilities in the following ways:

  • Increased Complexity: Managing multiple disabilities can be more challenging, as each condition may require different types of support and interventions.
  • Impact on Functioning: Psychosocial disabilities can affect a person's ability to manage other disabilities. For example, someone with a physical disability might find it harder to cope if they are also dealing with depression or anxiety.
  • Support Needs: The presence of psychosocial disability may change the type or level of support a person needs for their other disabilities. They might need additional emotional or social support to handle both conditions effectively.
  • Barrier Reinforcement: Psychosocial disabilities can exacerbate the barriers faced by individuals with other disabilities, making it harder to access services, maintain employment, or participate in social activities.
  • Cumulative Effects: The combination of psychosocial and other disabilities can lead to a greater overall impact on a person's life, potentially reducing their quality of life and increasing their need for comprehensive, coordinated care.

CHCAGE013* / *CHCDIS020*

38. Psychosocial disability

Psychosocial disability refers to the challenges faced by individuals who have limitations in their daily life due to mental health conditions. Not everyone with a mental health condition experiences psychosocial disability.

CHCAGE013*

39. Impacts of psychosocial disability

Psychosocial disability could affect someone's working memory, making it hard for them to organize daily tasks. It might also make it difficult for them to shop, spend time with friends, and keep appointments. Another person close to them may also be affected because they would need to help to support and take care of things at home.

CHCAGE013* / *CHCDIS020*

40. Additional Supports

  • Transportation: Helping someone get to appointments like doctors and psychologists.
  • Personal Care Assistance: Assisting with personal care needs.
  • Work and Community Support: Supporting attendance at work or accessing the community.
  • Housing Assistance: Assisting in finding or maintaining housing.
  • Relationship Support: Providing support to maintain relationships.
  • Increased Support: The level of support increases during these times.

*CHCDIS020**CHCDIS020*
